summary: Specifies a way to give FTP data ports addresses other than 32-bit IPv4 ones, using a long port command and a long passive reply. It is an experimental protocol.

eli5.summary: FTP only knew short addresses. This adds longer ones so it can work with other kinds of networks.

questions: what does foobar mean in ftp
subtitle: Experimental FTP commands that let data connections use addresses other than 32-bit IPv4 ones.

tldr.problem: FTP's PORT command and PASV reply can only describe a 32-bit IPv4 address and a 16-bit TCP port, which does not fit larger or non-IP addresses.
tldr.mechanism: It adds a LPRT command and a LPSV reply, each carrying an address family, a length-prefixed host address and a length-prefixed port, plus reply code 521 for unsupported families.
tldr.outcome: It is an Experimental protocol that obsoletes RFC 1545 and does not specify an Internet standard of any kind.

today: RFC 1639 is an Experimental protocol that obsoletes RFC 1545. According to its metadata, it has not been obsoleted or updated by a later RFC.

sections.title: Why PORT and PASV Fall Short
sections.content:
In the File Transfer Protocol (RFC 959), the PORT command names the data port for a data connection, and the PASV reply asks the server to listen on a data port. Its <host-port> argument is a 32-bit internet host address plus a 16-bit TCP port, sent as 8-bit decimal fields separated by commas, as in PORT h1,h2,h3,h4,p1,p2.

To handle the larger addresses expected from "next generation" IP alternatives, and network and transport protocols other than IP, new commands and reply codes are needed.
sections.eli5: FTP's address slot was only big enough for short addresses, like a form with room for a four-number phone number. Longer addresses would not fit.

sections.title: The LPRT Command
sections.content:
The LPRT command has the form LPRT <SP> <long-host-port> <CRLF>. The long argument concatenates an 8-bit address family (af), an 8-bit host address length (hal), a host address of that length, an 8-bit port address length (pal) and a port address of that length.

It is written as unsigned decimal fields separated by commas: LPRT af,hal,h1,h2,h3,h4...,pal,p1,p2.... Negative numbers are explicitly not permitted. Values 0 to 15 of the address family are reserved for IP and assigned by IANA, and 16 to 255 are available for IANA to assign to other network layer protocols.
sections.eli5: The new command says what kind of address it is, how long the address is, then the address, then how long the port is, then the port.

sections.title: LPSV and the New Reply Codes
sections.content:
The Long Passive reply works like PASV but with a long address. It uses reply code 228, with suggested text 228 Entering Long Passive Mode (af, hal, h1, h2, h3,..., pal, p1, p2...).

The existing syntax-error codes 500 and 501 also fit LPRT and LPSV. A new code, 521, is for a host that supports the commands but not the address family requested. Its suggested text is 521 Supported address families are (af1, af2, ..., afn).
sections.eli5: When the server listens for a connection it can now reply with a longer address. If it does not understand the address kind, it says which kinds it does understand.

sections.title: Rationale and Status
sections.content:
An explicit address family lets the community experiment with various next generation IP and other network layer protocols within one FTP implementation, and it also allows a different address family on the command and data connections. A host address length is needed because some alternatives use variable length addresses. The port length goes beyond what TCP requires, but one IPng alternative (TP/IX) supports longer port addresses, and other transports may exceed 16 bits.

The memo concludes that the mechanism is simple, extensible, and meets both IPNG and multi-protocol internet needs. It is an Experimental protocol, it obsoletes RFC 1545, and its Security Considerations section says security issues are not discussed.
sections.eli5: The authors made the address slot stretchy so it can hold many future kinds of addresses, not only the ones known today.
